name: Borderline personality disorder (borderline pattern)
dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Personality Disorders — Borderline Personality Disorder; ICD-11 rates personality disorder severity with an optional borderline pattern specifier.
summary: A long-standing pattern of intense, fast-changing emotions, fear of being left, stormy relationships, an unsteady sense of self and impulsive or self-damaging acts, often including self-harm and suicidal crises. Emotions rise quickly in response to interpersonal events and take a long time to settle. The pattern usually begins in adolescence or early adulthood and is often linked to early adversity, though not always. It is treatable: structured therapies such as DBT, MBT and schema therapy reduce self-harm and improve functioning, and many people improve substantially over the years. Avoid labeling during an acute crisis or after a single meeting, and use the term with care because of stigma. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: A personality pattern is long-standing and shows up across settings. Look for it over years, not only during a crisis, and check DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 for guidance on assessment.

ruleOuts.label: Substance intoxication and withdrawal
ruleOuts.note: Alcohol and drugs can cause impulsivity and mood shifts; assess patterns when sober. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Neurological causes of personality change
ruleOuts.note: Head injury, seizures or other brain conditions can change emotional control; ask about onset after an injury or illness.

ruleOuts.label: Bipolar spectrum disorder
ruleOuts.note: Look for days-long highs with reduced need for sleep rather than shifts lasting hours.

ruleOuts.label: Complex trauma responses
ruleOuts.note: Trauma-related emotional dysregulation and relationship difficulties overlap; ICD-11 complex PTSD (6B41) is a differential.

specifiers.label: ICD-11 severity: mild, moderate or severe (descriptive)
specifiers.note: ICD-11 rates overall personality disorder severity (6D10.0 to 6D10.2) with the borderline pattern specifier 6D11.5. See DSM-5-TR for its categorical approach.

differentials.label: Bipolar II disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Discrete days-long highs with less need for sleep, not hour-to-hour shifts.

differentials.label: Posttraumatic stress disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Intrusions and avoidance tied to a trauma; complex trauma can add emotional and relationship difficulties.

differentials.label: Major depressive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: A clear episode of low mood that differs from the client's usual pattern.

differentials.label: Adult ADHD
differentials.distinguishing: Impulsivity without the fear of abandonment and identity disturbance.

comorbidities.label: Depression
comorbidities.note: Very common; treat both and track suicide risk closely.

comorbidities.label: Trauma
comorbidities.note: Many clients have trauma histories; stabilization skills usually come before trauma processing.

comorbidities.label: Substance use
comorbidities.note: Common and linked to higher risk; screen sensitively.

comorbidities.label: Eating disorders
comorbidities.note: Binge-purge patterns can co-occur; ask about eating.

measuresPending.name: McLean Screening Instrument for Borderline Personality Disorder (MSI-BPD)

interventions.name: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT)
interventions.evidence: Linehan et al. (2006) found DBT halved suicide attempts compared with therapy by experts; NICE CG78 supports DBT for women with recurrent self-harm.
interventions.note: Comprehensive DBT includes individual therapy, skills group, coaching and a consultation team; individual skills can be taught as an adjunct.

interventions.name: Mentalization-based treatment (MBT)
interventions.evidence: Outpatient MBT reduced self-harm and hospital admissions more than structured clinical management (Bateman and Fonagy, 2009).

interventions.name: Schema therapy
interventions.evidence: Schema-focused therapy outperformed transference-focused psychotherapy on recovery in Giesen-Bloo et al. (2006); a 2023 meta-analysis (Zhang et al.) supports it across personality disorders.

interventions.name: Collaborative safety planning
interventions.evidence: Recommended for anyone with self-harm or suicidal crises.
interventions.note: Build a crisis plan with the client; this app never rates risk.

interventions.name: Medication referral for co-occurring conditions
interventions.evidence: NICE CG78 does not recommend medication for the pattern itself; it can treat co-occurring conditions.
interventions.note: Refer to a prescriber for depression, anxiety or other conditions.

culturalNotes: Emotional expression, closeness and independence are judged differently across cultures and generations. Interpret intensity and relationship patterns against the client's own context.
The label carries stigma, and women are more often given it than men with a similar picture. Describe the pattern and its treatability, and invite the client's view.
Many clients have experienced abuse, neglect, racism or discrimination. Name these experiences as context, not as character flaws.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.
If the client wants faith or spiritual practice included, follow their lead and get informed consent first (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors); never impose beliefs.

redFlagRules.message: Suicidal thoughts or self-harm are documented in this input. Ask directly about intent, plan and access to means, follow your crisis protocol and build a safety plan with the client; this app never rates risk.
Psychotic symptoms are documented. Brief stress-related paranoia can occur in this pattern, but persistent hallucinations or delusions need an urgent psychiatric evaluation.
